#general > LANA project announcement @ 💬

David Michael Roberts said:

If the LANA team is implementing species and mutations etc, I'd really, really hope they aren't going to work with isomorphism classes of functors, but the actual 2-categorical structure. In this category theorist's opinion, that single step did an act of violence on what seems to be trying to happen.

Does anybody understand why it is so important that ZFC be formalised in FOL, rather than in Lean's metalogic, for IUT? I am very lost on this point.

I know nothing about the LANA project or algebraic geometry, but since formalizing ZFC is far easier than formalizing Lean’s metatheory (which we did in #Formalized Formal Logic) I do not think it is particularly strange to consider ZFC (more precisely formulas of set theory), as an option when one wants to deal with things like the definability of mathematical structures with high expressive power.

Let me put on my anabelian-geometer hat on (as opposed to my "LANA member hat"). Anabelian geometry is a subject where we "construct stuff". Probably the most well-known theorem in the subject is the Neukirch-Uchida theorem which states (among other things) that whenever KKK and LLL are number fields with chosen algebraic closures Kˉ\bar KKˉ and Lˉ\bar LLˉ, any isomorphism of Galois groups Gal(Kˉ∣K)≅Gal(Lˉ∣L)Gal(\bar K|K) \cong Gal(\bar L | L)Gal(Kˉ∣K)≅Gal(Lˉ∣L) arises from an isomorphism of (etale-pointed) fields Kˉ∣K≅Lˉ∣L\bar K | K \cong \bar L | LKˉ∣K≅Lˉ∣L in the natural way.

One can phrase this as an assertion that some functor (Gal(−)Gal(-)Gal(−) restricted to the appropriate category) is fully-faithful. But such an assertion is fundamentally different from the assertion that there is some "recipe" that starts with the profinite group Gal(Kˉ∣K)Gal(\bar K | K)Gal(Kˉ∣K) and constructs the fields Kˉ∣K\bar K | KKˉ∣K. To phrase such a thing precisely, one should indeed use concepts from logic (e.g. interpretability in the sense of model theory, or something along those lines), as this distinction is a meta assertion.
In fact, in this particular example, a recipe that constructs the number fields only came about much later than the original theorem (and is due to Hoshi).

Going a bit deeper, if you take the Neukirch-Uchida theorem as a given, and you're given a profinite group GGG which you just so happen to know is isomorphic to Gal(Kˉ∣K)Gal(\bar K | K)Gal(Kˉ∣K) for a number field KKK, you could proceed with the following naive recipe: Quantify over all Lˉ∣L\bar L |LLˉ∣L, and check whether Gal(Lˉ∣L)Gal(\bar L|L)Gal(Lˉ∣L) is isomorphic to GGG. The theorem tells you that all such Lˉ∣L\bar L|LLˉ∣L which satisfy this condition are isomorphic to Kˉ∣K\bar K|KKˉ∣K, so you could say: look, I recovered Kˉ∣K\bar K|KKˉ∣K up to isomorphism from GGG!

The main point here is the following: if you have a fully-faithful essentially surjective functor F:C→DF : C \to DF:C→D between two categories, then you know that it is an equivalence. Using the axiom of choice, you can (non-constructively!) obtain an essential inverse G:D→CG : D \to CG:D→C. Alternatively, you may want to construct G:D→CG : D \to CG:D→C in some more precise way and show that it is an essential inverse. If you only care about the fact that FFF is an equivalence but you don't care at all about the implementation of GGG, then either is fine. But sometimes you do care about the implementation of GGG.

Now let's bring Lean into the picture. One reason we may want to care about the implementation of GGG is to be able to use the definitional properties of GGG (e.g. we may want to use rfl to prove something about GGG). If we construct GGG using choice using only the fact that FFF is fully faithful and essentially surjective, we will lose all definitional properties about GGG. If we instead construct GGG carefully, then in principle it is possible to use rfl to prove things about it.

Thanks for this. In terms of the distinction between existence and definability: I don't quite understand why we need another formalism. Surely you can just write down your defeq-correct construction directly in Lean's logic?
Yes, I agree.

If you want to start reasoning (i.e. proving theorems) about implementations of things like GGG in Lean, then (just like you do on paper!) you need to use things like formulas, etc.. But if you just want to mimic informal proofs that say "this follows from the definition" (i.e. by rfl), then writing down a definition with good defeq properties is all you need.
Is Mochizuki trying to reason about the implementation? I didn't get that from his talk (although I admit I did struggle to follow it).

My impression is that he is doing meta-reasoning in the sense of by rfl (in which case using Lean's type theory directly is fine) but not in the sense of "the implementation of this algorithm uses three existential quantifiers" (which would require a deep embedding of the logic).
But this is just my impression.
thanks again for the detailed explanation

But such an assertion is fundamentally different from the assertion that there is some "recipe" that starts with the profinite group Gal(Kˉ∣K)Gal(\bar K | K)Gal(Kˉ∣K) and constructs the fields Kˉ∣K\bar K | KKˉ∣K. To phrase such a thing precisely, one should indeed use concepts from logic (e.g. interpretability in the sense of model theory, or something along those lines), as this distinction is a meta assertion.

sorry for lagging behind but I still don't get the point. I totally understand and agree that there's a difference between "this exists by Exists.choose and "this exists because I just made it" but what do you mean by "To phrase such a thing precisely, one should indeed use concepts from logic"? Why aren't you saying "To phrase such a thing more precisely one should make a def bottom_field G and def top_field G and then prove Gal(top_field/bottom_field) is isomorphic to G"? What has logic got to do with this?
@Kevin Buzzard the main point is that if you want a type whose terms are "recipes" of the sort I mention above, then this type would be defined in terms of logical formulas in some way.

For example, here is an example of a type of "recipes" of functions in one variable that make sense for semirings:

import Mathlib.Algebra.Ring.Defs

inductive SemiringRecipe where
  | var : SemiringRecipe
  | zero : SemiringRecipe
  | one : SemiringRecipe
  | add : SemiringRecipe → SemiringRecipe → SemiringRecipe
  | mul : SemiringRecipe → SemiringRecipe → SemiringRecipe

def SemiringRecipe.eval {A : Type*} [Semiring A] : SemiringRecipe → A → A
  | var, a => a
  | zero, _ => 0
  | one, _ => 1
  | add x y, a => x.eval a + y.eval a
  | mul x y, a => x.eval a * y.eval a

and you can think of SemiringRecipe as (essentially) the type of quantifier-free formulas in one variable in the language of semirings.

With SemiringRecipe I can write down theorems like "this particular implementation of function so-and-so from a semiring to itself involves addition precisely three times". This is an example of a theorem that you can state if you have a type that lets you reason about implementations, but which can't really be stated in any other way.

My original comment perhaps didn't highlight the part I found especially dubious: the claim that "how fundamental ZFC as a first order theory is throughout pure mathematics".

@Adam Topaz so can one do this in eg the multi-sorted Lawevere theory for rings? Seems to me like using ZFC as a first-order theory and doing it syntactically is massive overkill. Obviously to get up to the point of profinite groups and whatnot, you need more machinery, but I can imagine doing this with localic groups that correspond to profinite groups, and so everything becomes rather algebraic, rather than fooling around with species of topological groups in the syntactic category of ZFC (I mean, does this machinery use AC, if everything is "algorithmic"? And I doubt it uses anything outside bounded Zermelo set theory....)

Is there something I can read about species and mutations, by the way? I'm afraid I didn't quite understand what they were and I haven't seen these words before (although I understand they're equivalent to categories and functors internal to a model of ZFC).
It's in Mochizuki's 4th IUT paper if you want to take a look.
Oh it's a concept by Mochizuki. Apologies, I thought it was used more widely among say logicians or category theorists.

But I would suggest rather thinking of species/mutations as internal categories/functors in a suitable category with finite limits. Mochizuki's definition is essentially this if you take the ambient category to be the syntactic category of ZFC.

Artie Khovanov said:

Oh it's a concept by Mochizuki. Apologies, I thought it was used more widely among say logicians or category theorists.

Yes, the terms "species" and "mutations" were introduced by Mochizuki, but as I said above, the concept is not new if you interpret it in the appropriate way.

I guess I have a new question
Why might we want to look at categories internal to the syntactic category of ZFC as a first-order logic in the course of ordinary (non-foundational) maths?
After all, ZFC is expressive enough to encode any mathematical theory, barring universe subtelties.

Artie Khovanov said:

After all, ZFC is expressive enough to encode any mathematical theory, barring universe subtelties.

this seems like a very fast generalization without proper basis to me... is there a theorem here, or is this some gut feeling/ philosophical standpoint? because i understand that from an empirical standpoint, this could be true, but that does feel like a big caviat to me...
If you're a mathematician for whom ZFC is the foundation of mathematics, then this is a tautology!
exactly, and obviously so, which is why stating this statement seems suspicious to me.

if you ascribe to the mentioned "ZFC is the foundation of mathematics", there's no point stating that, and if you agree that there could be some other foundation/multiple foundations of mathematics, it becomes very non-obvious how you could argue that "all mathematical theories can be encoded in mathematical theory X"
We're not talking about some crazy model of mathematical reasoning here - we're talking about anabelian geometry. Mochizuki himself is saying he is proving ZFC-valid theorems.

In this context it's not clear to me why we are looking at categories in the syntactic category of ZFC as a first order theory rather than just, well, class sized categories, or U-small categories where U is a ZFC universe.
Sorry, but I lost track of what the point of this thread is…

For what it's worth Mochizuki wrote a lot more about his ideas about formalising species and mutations than in the pdf document, and how incredibly central and important doing this is, in his blog post of the 1st Jan this year https://plaza.rakuten.co.jp/shinichi0329/

I cannot stress how much I disagree with the idea that pure mathematics generically sees the use of ZFC syntactic encoding of structures as so important as M. makes it out to be.

I know this is not speaking for LANA, but I really would like to know if what is done with species (under whatever name the idea goes by in practice outside Mochizuki's work) can really be done in the syntactic category of Zermelo set theory. Does anyone actually need transfinite iterations of power sets, for instance? Is AC actually used in the syntax for these "functorial algorithms"? Obviously in the metatheory one can have AC, but if the point is to actually describe constructions based on input data, I cannot see how AC (or the stronger version, the Hilbert epsilon/Bourbaki tau operator) should ever be use.

I get the impression that M. thinks that the Lean people working on formalisation somehow just chose or merely prefer formalising using type theory over ZFC. I note however that this blog post is months old and one hopes that in the back-and-forth since he has been disabused of this notion.

I get the impression that M. thinks that the Lean people working on formalisation somehow just chose or merely prefer formalising using type theory over ZFC.

I mean, surely that's true for at least some of us? (It is for me.)
No, I mean they choose to use use Lean, and subsequently to that, choose to work in type theory and not ZFC. Not that they choose Lean because it's based on type theory.
I'm sorry for writing it in a misleading way!

OK, I watched Mochizuki's talk at AITPM, and I'm glad to hear that someone who is experienced in Lean convinced him that he doesn't need to formalise the syntactic category of ZFC in order to define species.

Ideally someone tells him about functorial semantics à la Lawvere, and things like sketches etc which more or less do what I think he wants.
@David Michael Roberts is there a relevant timestamp?
@Adam Topaz I'll check

@Adam Topaz starting here:

And so here we observe that the technical significance of formalising ZFC as a first order theory lies in the fact that it is necessary in order to be able to work with some indeterminate set theoretic formula phi as opposed to specific set theoretic formulas like a contained in A and so on. which are natively available in Lean. So, this was something that I spent a certain amount of time on last fall, but as a result of various consultations with Lean experts, I finally reached the conclusion that the formalisation of species or mutations in the abstract using some sort of Lean formalisation of ZFC as a first order theory, although this would ultimately be theoretically desirable at perhaps some later stage in the project, was most likely not necessary for the Lean formalisation of at least stages one to two of IUT, that instead one could use standard Lean commands for formalising types of mathematical objects and relationships between various respective components, component pieces of data, and the input output of a functor. So this seems to be sufficient for formalising the logic of IUT, at least at the stages, in the case of stages one and two.

and here:

Question: So you mentioned Lean doesn't have a formalisation of ZFC as a first order logic. Can you expand on that and why it's important for IUT? And I wonder whether also you might just comment on whether, why the choice of Lean, if that's the case as well.

Answer: Well, so I was told by a Lean expert, I'm not an expert on the content of Mathlib, but I was told that it doesn't currently exist in Mathlib, but on the other hand, it's something that's not particularly difficult, and so it's not that it doesn't exist in Mathlib because it's terribly difficult to do, but because it just doesn't, people haven't been sufficiently interested in doing it, at least for Mathlib, and so, so the reason that it is relevant for IUT is because one needs to talk about types of mathematical objects and algorithms that construct one kind of mathematical object from another. And so from the point of view of usual mathematics, the only way to define these kinds of notions is by using set theoretic formulas. And that's where ZFC as a first order theory comes in. But from the point of view of Lean, and of course, I'm not, Yeah. I'm very far from being an expert on the structure of Lean, but the point is that by using types and various other sort of standard features The. of Lean, one can... In some sense, express the logic that... Um... that is used when one considers species and mutations without actually explicitly talking about set-theoretic formulas. Although, as I said, I think that it's theoretically desirable that at some point someone does this in terms of the set-theoretic formulas. which was the original mathematics, the original way it was written in the papers. But from the point of view of expressing the logic of arguments involving species and mutations, one can in fact, at least as far as I can see, use standard Lean commands to Express this logic, yeah.
